bib.title: A Survey of Hallucination in Large Foundation Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "A Survey of Hallucination in 'Large' Foundation Models", Vipula Rawte, Amit Sheth, Amitava Das (AI Institute, University of South Carolina). Preprint: the only venue mark on the PDF is "arXiv:2309.05922v1 [cs.AI] 12 Sep 2023". Year 2023.
File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/sources/rawte-2023-survey-hallucination-large-foundation-models.pdf

COVERAGE: 11 of 11 pages, 40,507 of 40,507 chars. Body is pp. 1-6, Table 1 is pp. 7-8, conclusion pp. 8-9, references pp. 9-11 (skimmed for origins). There are no appendices. Page numbers below are derived from character offsets, so treat them as plus or minus one page.

DOES IT CONTRIBUTE ANYTHING OF ITS OWN? Very little.
- It has no experiments and no numbers of its own. Every figure in it is restated from a cited paper.
- Its "taxonomy" (Fig. 1) is a grouping of about 25 papers by modality (text, image, video, audio), with text split into LLMs, multilingual and domain-specific. It is not a taxonomy of hallucination types, although the abstract says the paper "classifies various types of hallucination phenomena".
- Its one reusable artefact is Table 1 (pp. 7-8): one row per paper, with columns Detect, Mitigate, Task(s), Dataset, Evaluation Metric.
- It gives a loose definition of hallucination and a one-sentence definition of grounding.
- The body is paraphrased abstracts. The abstract's claim that it "establishes evaluation criteria" is not delivered.

CLAIMS
- claim: Hallucination is defined as content not based on factual information.
  number: none
  setup: definitional; no intrinsic/extrinsic or faithfulness/factuality split
  quote: "Hallucination in the context of a foundation model refers to a situation where the model generates content that is not based on factual or accurate information."
  where: p. 1, sec. 1.2
- claim: Grounding is defined as connecting generated text to structured knowledge.
  number: none
  setup: describing Chain of Knowledge (Li et al., 2023d)
  quote: "Grounding refers to the process of connecting LLM-generated text with structured knowledge to improve factual accuracy and reliability."
  where: p. 4, sec. 2.1
- claim: A leading vision-language model hallucinates in about 30 percent of its detailed descriptions.
  number: 30 percent; 16,000 annotations
  setup: InstructBLIP on VQA examples, as reported by Gunjal et al. 2023 (M-HalDetect); secondhand
  quote: "Even state-of-the-art LVLMs like InstructBLIP exhibit a high rate of hallucinatory text, comprising 30 percent of non-existent objects, inaccurate descriptions, and erroneous relationships." and "M-HalDetect contains 16,000 finely detailed annotations on VQA examples"
  where: p. 5, sec. 3
- claim: Most model-written video caption sentences contain factual errors, and n-gram metrics do not track human judgement.
  number: 57.0%
  setup: human evaluation in Liu and Wan 2023 (ActivityNet Captions, YouCook2 per Table 1); secondhand
  quote: "revealing that 57.0% of model-generated sentences contain factual errors. Existing evaluation metrics, mainly based on n-gram matching, do not align well with human assessments."
  where: p. 6, sec. 4
- claim: Hybrid retrieval reduces hallucination compared with vector-only retrieval in a legal LLM.
  number: none
  setup: ChatLaw (Cui et al., 2023); asserted, no measurement given
  quote: "they propose a method that combines vector database retrieval with keyword retrieval. This approach effectively reduces inaccuracies that may arise when solely relying on vector database retrieval"
  where: p. 4, sec. 2.3
- claim: Smaller open-source LLMs hallucinate more than larger ones.
  number: none (BLOOM 7B is the model named)
  setup: Elaraby et al. 2023 (HaloCheck), secondhand
  quote: "Smaller, open-source LLMs with fewer parameters often experience significant hallucination issues compared to their larger counterparts (Elaraby et al., 2023)."
  where: p. 4
- claim: Table 1 pairs methods with datasets and metrics relevant to the note: RARR and PURR ("Editing for Attribution", metric "Attributable to Identified Sources"), SelfCheckGPT (WikiBio), Chain of Knowledge (FEVER, AdvHotpotQA, accuracy), LLM-Augmenter (Knowledge F1, BLEU-4), Varshney et al. (WikiBio, percentage of mitigated hallucinations).
  number: none
  setup: listing only, no results
  quote: "RARR: Researching and Revising What Language Models Say, Using Language Models (Gao et al., 2023) Editing for Attribution NQ, SQA, QReCC Attributable to Iden- tified Sources"
  where: pp. 7-8
- claim: An LP-MusicCaps dataset size is restated (not a hallucination result).
  number: 2.2 million captions, 0.5 million clips
  quote: "comprising around 2.2 million captions paired with 0.5 million audio clips"
  where: p. 6, sec. 5

LIMITS
- No limitations section, and no stated inclusion criteria or search method.
- It shows nothing about retrieval metrics, claim-by-claim faithfulness scoring, grounding tiers, or how detectors compare with each other. Table 1 lists metrics without any scores.
- Coverage is March to September 2023 (Fig. 2), so it is dated.
- Several included papers are not about hallucination as an error: Wu et al.'s "Hallucinator" for contrastive learning, Kulal's person insertion, Yu's video inpainting, VideoChat, LP-MusicCaps and Audio-Journey.
- Section 7 (future directions) is generic and drifts into bias and regulation.

BUILDS ON: Ji et al. 2023 (survey of hallucination in NLG, ACM Computing Surveys) and Zhang et al. 2023c ("Siren's Song", survey of LLM hallucination) are credited as the prior surveys; this one claims to be the first across all modalities. Bommasani et al. 2021 is credited for "foundation model".

CODE: none.

FIGURES: At most one candidate, and it is weak. Figure 1, p. 3, "Taxonomy for Hallucination in Large Foundation Models": a quick map of which 2023 papers sit under which modality. Table 1 (pp. 7-8) is more useful than any figure, but see PROBLEMS.

PROBLEMS
- Table 1's Detect and Mitigate tick/cross glyphs were lost in extraction, so those two columns cannot be read from the text; they need a visual check of pp. 7-8.
- No embedded instructions were found.
- The source has citation faults visible in its own pages:
  - "Attributable to Identified Sources" is cited to "Castaldo and Yang, 2007", which the reference list shows is a sepsis paper in The American Surgeon.
  - The multilingual translation study is cited as Pfeiffer et al. 2023, but that reference entry is the mmT5 paper, while Table 1 titles the row "Hallucinations in Large Multilingual Translation Models".
  - HaluEval appears in the references as "Helma".
  - Sec. 2 points to "Fig. 4" for LLM hallucination, but Fig. 4 is the vision-language example.
  - Sec. 3 says "we introduce the Hallucinator", which is abstract text carried over from Wu et al.
- Table 1 gives SelfCheckGPT's metric as "Token probability or entropy", which describes a baseline rather than a metric. Do not use this survey as the source for SelfCheckGPT details; the note already cites the original.
